title: "Number of ratings, rater differences, and score reliability in creativity ratings of football actions: A judge response theory analysis"

abstract: |
  The consensual assessment technique (CAT) is the standard procedure for rating creative products and is increasingly applied to actions in sport. However, it is unknown how many ratings an action needs for a reliable creativity score, and how much raters differ when they judge creativity in sport. In this exploratory study, 19 student raters gave 7820 ratings of 3668 football actions on a 7-point creativity scale. We fitted judge response theory models by marginal maximum likelihood, comparing a graded response model (GRM) with an adjacent-category ladder from the many-facet Rasch model to the generalized partial credit model, and projected score reliability from the fitted GRM. The empirical reliability of the obtained scores was .672, against .960 for a hypothetical full panel. In the projection, one rating from randomly drawn raters gave a reliability of .508, whereas one rating from the most informative raters gave .754. Among raters with at least 400 ratings, discrimination ranged from 0.86 to 2.81; raters also differed in threshold location and category use. Likelihood-ratio tests rejected a shared category structure and equal discrimination (both *p* < .001). Raw mean ratings and GRM scores agreed only partly (Kendall's $\tau_b$ = .796), and with a single rating, the same rating corresponded to GRM scores up to 1.436 apart. For this kind of rater pool, creativity studies in sport should plan both the number of ratings per action and who gives them, link raters through a common calibration set, and model rater differences rather than average them. # Introduction

Creativity is widely regarded as one of the core competencies of the modern world. Employers rank creative thinking among the core skills of the workforce [@worldeconomicforum2025] [\[FILL IN: verify this wording against the report; also verify the framing claims attributed to safardilha2019, memmert2011, batey2012 and barbot2019b against the PDFs (FI-17)\]]{.mark}, and the Programme for International Student Assessment assessed creative thinking as an innovative domain in its 2022 cycle [@oecd2024]. In sport, creativity is considered a key quality to be developed and evaluated in players [@safardilha2019; @santos2016]. Assessing creativity validly and reliably is therefore a basic task, in society in general and in sport in particular.

Creativity research distinguishes four facets of creativity: the creative person, the creative process, the creative product and the press, that is, the environment in which creativity occurs [@batey2012]. Each facet requires its own measurement approach [@barbot2019; @barbot2019b]. The present paper is concerned with the product facet, namely actions performed in football matches, and with the evaluation of these actions by others.

The consensual assessment technique (CAT) is the established method for evaluating creative products [@amabile1982; @hennessey2011; @kaufman2024]. In the CAT and judge response theory literature, raters are called judges; we use "raters" throughout. In the CAT, raters who are familiar with the domain rate products independently and relative to one another [@amabile1982; @hennessey2011]. Although the procedure rests on subjective judgements, independent raters usually reach coefficient alphas above .70 [@baer2004; @kaufman2008; @hennessey2011] [\[FILL IN: verify the ".70" claim against the PDFs (FI-17)\]]{.mark}. Considerably lower agreement has also been reported, however, and has been attributed to differences between raters in rating procedure, in their use of the rating scale and in their beliefs about creativity [@long2015; @cseh2019].

The reliability of CAT scores rests on the number of raters. As already noted by @amabile1982, the Spearman–Brown reliability of an aggregated rating depends jointly on the mean inter-rater correlation and on the number of raters, so that a larger panel compensates for lower agreement between individual raters. Conversely, a high alpha obtained from a large panel can mask low agreement among individual raters [@kaufman2008]. A rule of thumb of five to ten raters is often cited [@kaufman2008a] [\[FILL IN: verify against the PDF (FI-17)\]]{.mark}, but @cseh2019 argue that the number of raters needed depends on the product and the domain and must therefore be established for each domain. A further distinction becomes important when many products are rated. A panel coefficient describes the mean over all raters of the panel. When each product receives only some of the possible ratings, what matters for the use of a score is the precision of each product's score given the ratings that this product actually received, and a fitted measurement model can project that precision for other numbers of ratings [@primi2019; @forthmann2023].

Raters also differ systematically. They differ in severity, in their use of the rating scale and in their beliefs about creativity [@long2015], and their tendencies can drift over time [@barth2020]. Research on rater-mediated assessment has described these differences as rater effects, including severity, central tendency, restriction of range and halo [@engelhard1994; @myford2003; @myford2004]. In judged sports, the accuracy and bias of judges have been monitored with Rasch-family or other statistical models, although for performance quality rather than for creativity [@looney2004; @anderlucci2021; @heiniger2021].

How such rater differences are handled depends on the scoring model, and the development from averaging to judge response theory (JRT) can be described as a successive relaxation of assumptions about raters. Three kinds of rater difference need to be kept apart. The first is severity. Mean scores treat raters as interchangeable, and whenever different raters rate different products, mean scores are confounded with the severity of the raters who happened to rate each product [@primi2019]. The many-facet Rasch model (MFRM) adds rater severity as a facet and thereby corrects for this confounding [@linacre1989; @eckes2015; @primi2019]. The second and third kinds are differences in category structure and in discrimination. Item response theory (IRT) models the probability of each response as a function of a latent attribute and of item parameters [@lord1980; @embretson2013; @deayala2022]. Rasch models constrain all items to discriminate equally [@rasch1960; @bond2020]; their polytomous extensions, the rating scale model [RSM, @andrich1978] and the partial credit model [PCM, @masters1982], differ in whether all items share one category structure. The MFRM thus still assumes a shared category structure and equal discrimination, so that differences in discrimination have no parameter and surface only as misfit [@myford2004; @myszkowski2021]. Mean scores and coefficient alpha additionally assume (essentially) $\tau$-equivalent raters [@myszkowski2019]. JRT treats raters as items with their own discrimination and thresholds, for instance in the generalized partial credit model [GPCM, @muraki1992] or the graded response model [GRM, @samejima1969], and yields scores with product-specific standard errors as well as an explicit description of rater behaviour [@myszkowski2019; @myszkowski2021]. JRT has been applied in recent creativity research [@barbot2023; @pellegrino2025], and @pellegrino2025 retained a GRM; simulation work has addressed planned-missing rating designs [@forthmann2023]. Two model families are available. The RSM, PCM and GPCM are adjacent-category models and nested, so that their constraints can be tested by likelihood-ratio tests. The GRM is a cumulative model, which arguably matches a scale on which raters express an increasing amount of creativity [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-8\]]{.mark}; the two families can be compared by information criteria.

Creativity research in sport has focused mainly on the creative process, for example on divergent thinking [@memmert2011]. Ratings of creative products, that is, of actions, exist as well. @kempe2018 obtained ratings of actions in competition from trained experts and found face validity in the proximity of the rated actions to goals; their scale originated in expert ratings of tactical creativity [@memmert2007]. Further studies have rated football actions [@zahno2023; @dejoode2023]. These studies average the ratings and report intraclass correlations or agreement only [\[FILL IN: verify this characterisation of kempe2018, zahno2023 and dejoode2023 against the PDFs (FI-17)\]]{.mark}; a Rasch validation exists only for a coach-completed creativity questionnaire that rates players rather than actions [@shin2025]. However, three gaps remain. First, there is no evidence on how many ratings per action are needed for a reliable creativity score in sport, which is the domain-specific evidence called for by @cseh2019. Second, there is no evidence on how raters differ when they judge the creativity of sport actions. Third, to our knowledge, no study has modelled such rater differences with IRT or JRT for creativity ratings in sport. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-2: the literature search was not systematic\]]{.mark}

## The present study

The present study analysed a large set of CAT-style creativity ratings of football actions given by multiple raters (see Methods and @tbl-design-summary). The study was exploratory and had three aims: (1) to describe how the reliability of creativity scores depends on the number of ratings, (2) to describe how raters differ, and (3) to describe how much the scores depend on whether rater differences are modelled. No confirmatory hypotheses were formulated; the following research questions (RQs) were answered descriptively. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-20: exploratory framing and RQ wording\]]{.mark}

- **RQ1 (number of ratings and reliability).** How does the reliability of creativity scores depend on the number of ratings per product (i.e., per action), and on which raters give them? How does the reliability of the scores actually obtained compare with the reliability of a hypothetical full panel and with conventional agreement and consistency indices?
- **RQ2 (rater differences).** How do raters differ in their rating behaviour, that is, in severity, scale use, discrimination and their contribution to information, and how precisely are these differences estimated?
- **RQ3 (dependence of the scores on modelling rater differences).** (a) Are the constraints that treat raters as equivalent in category structure (RSM/MFRM) and in discrimination (PCM) tenable for these ratings? (b) How far do product scores and rankings change when rater differences are ignored (raw mean ratings) or constrained (RSM/MFRM, PCM, GPCM)?

To answer these questions, we fitted a ladder of JRT models and a GRM by marginal maximum likelihood, estimated the reliability of the scores actually obtained, projected the reliability for different numbers of ratings and choices of raters from the fitted model, described the rater parameters with their uncertainty, and compared GRM scores with raw mean ratings. Rater expertise and the design of the rating scale are not analysed in this paper.

# Methods

## Overview and study context

This was a CAT-style rating study in which raters independently rated the creativity of football actions in a randomised order [@amabile1982; @hennessey2011]. The ratings were collected as part of a larger project. [\[FILL IN: context and purpose of the larger project (FI-1, FI-2)\]]{.mark} [\[FILL IN: ethics approval (committee, reference number) and informed-consent procedure (FI-1)\]]{.mark} The analyses reported here were exploratory. [\[FILL IN: preregistration status, e.g., a statement that the study was not preregistered (FI-15)\]]{.mark}

## Raters

Raters were Bachelor's and Master's students who rated as part of their thesis projects. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; FI-1\]]{.mark} [\[FILL IN: recruitment and number of raters at the start (FI-1)\]]{.mark} [\[FILL IN: rater-pool description - football playing or coaching experience, any instruction or practice before rating, number of sessions per rater, demographics and compensation, or a statement that these were not recorded (FI-21)\]]{.mark} The final data comprised 19 raters, who gave between 50 and 1174 ratings each (@tbl-design-summary). Raters were pseudonymised as R01 to R19; the three excluded raters (see Data preparation and final data) are R20 to R22.

## Products and stimulus material

Each rated product was a single football action. Actions were shown as video clips from recorded football matches and were identified with event data. [\[FILL IN: competitions and matches (the project notes mention FIFA, AFCON, UEFA and Copa América matches with StatsBomb event data; to be verified), the action-selection rule, clip length, video source and number of matches (FI-2)\]]{.mark}

## Rating procedure

[\[FILL IN: rating software (FI-3)\]]{.mark} Raters were shown an instruction that defined creativity as the combination of originality and functionality of an action in its game context [@runco2012]. [\[FILL IN: verbatim instruction and creativity definition, original language and English translation (FI-3)\]]{.mark} Showing a definition departs to a minor degree from the CAT rule that raters receive no criteria [@hennessey2011], and resembles the procedure of trained-rater studies in sport [@kempe2018; @memmert2007]. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-19\]]{.mark} Creativity was rated on a unipolar 7-point scale with verbal anchors at 1, 4 and 7. [\[FILL IN: verify the anchors and give their wording (FI-3)\]]{.mark} In addition, raters could mark a clip as "action not recognised". [\[FILL IN: exact wording of the "not recognised" option (FI-3)\]]{.mark} Products were presented in a randomised order. [\[FILL IN: randomisation procedure, session length and breaks, and the data-collection period (timespan) (FI-3)\]]{.mark} Raters also rated technical correctness and aesthetic appeal, which are not analysed here. [\[FILL IN: wording and scales of the other rated dimensions (FI-3)\]]{.mark}

## Rating design

[\[FILL IN: how products were allocated to raters - planned overlap between raters, any common or benchmark set, randomisation, thesis-specific subsets or rater dropout; how products came to have 1, 2 or 3+ ratings; whether products with 4 or more ratings differ systematically (match, action type, rater composition); and how the additional ratings will be allocated (FI-4)\]]{.mark} Not every rater rated every product. The design was therefore incomplete but connected: all raters and products formed a single connected component, so that all rater parameters and product scores could be placed on one scale (@tbl-design-summary). Marginal maximum likelihood estimation assumes that the missing ratings are ignorable given the design. ## Data preparation and final data

The raw export contained 9148 rows. The 1290 ratings marked "action not recognised" were removed; such ratings result from video cutting and imperfect material, where close-ups or other TV artefacts render the action non-visible. [\[FILL IN: rate of "action not recognised" ratings by rater and, if available, whether they concentrate on particular products (FI-22)\]]{.mark} One out-of-range value (0.0, given by R04) was removed. Twelve rater–product pairs had been entered more than once, one of them with conflicting values; for each pair, the last entry was kept, which removed 13 rows. This left 7844 ratings by 22 raters.

Three raters gave fewer than 15 ratings: R20 (13 ratings), R21 (9) and R22 (2), together 24 ratings (@tbl-excluded-raters). Raters with fewer than 15 ratings were excluded because their up to seven rater-specific parameters cannot be estimated reliably. [\[FILL IN: source or rationale for the cut-off of 15 ratings (FI-23)\]]{.mark} The cut-off served as a technical estimation criterion only. Excluding these raters did not change the scores [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-26: alternatively "changed them negligibly"\]]{.mark}; the largest change in a product score was 0.16246 (@tbl-sensitivity-rater-exclusion; see Sensitivity to the rater exclusion in the Results). One product that had been rated only by the excluded raters was dropped.

@tbl-design-summary describes the final data on which all models were fitted: 7820 ratings of 3668 products by 19 raters. Ratings were given on the scale 1–7 and coded 0–6 internally. Products received a mean of 2.132 ratings (median 2, range 1–10, harmonic mean 1.726). The product-by-rater matrix had a fill of .112 and formed one connected component; 17 of the 171 rater pairs had no product in common, and the median overlap between rater pairs was 13 products. The distribution of the number of ratings per product is shown in @fig-overview-degree-distributions.

Five raters left categories at the top of the scale unused: category 7 was never used by R01, R03, R06 and R18, and categories 6 and 7 were never used by R17 (@tbl-category-usage). No rater left a category inside their observed range unused. Because the models estimate thresholds only between categories that a rater actually used, these raters have fewer thresholds.

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#tbl-design-summary >}}

## Measurement models

All models share the JRT frame [@myszkowski2019; @myszkowski2021]. Raters take the role of items and products the role of persons, and the creativity of products is a single latent dimension $\theta$ with a standard normal distribution. A rater's threshold $b_k$ is the $\theta$ at which a rating above category $k$ becomes more likely than a rating of $k$ or below, so that higher thresholds indicate a stricter rater; scale use is expressed by the spacing of the thresholds; and the discrimination $a$ expresses how sharply a rater's ratings separate products of different creativity. In the GRM, thresholds are expressed relative to discrimination, so that a rater with low discrimination has widely spaced thresholds. Threshold spacing is therefore partly the same fact as discrimination and is not read as separate evidence of scale use. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-6\]]{.mark}

The adjacent-category ladder comprised three nested models. M1 was the RSM [@andrich1978], which is equivalent to a two-facet MFRM with products and raters as facets [@linacre1989; @eckes2015; @primi2019]; it gives each rater a severity but assumes a shared category structure and equal discrimination. M1 was estimated with `sirt::rm.facets` [@robitzsch2025]. [\[FILL IN: how sirt treats raters with unused end categories (R01, R03, R06, R17, R18) under the shared category structure of M1 (FI-25)\]]{.mark} M2 was the PCM [@masters1982], which gives each rater their own thresholds, and M3 was the GPCM [@muraki1992], which additionally gives each rater their own discrimination. M2 and M3 were estimated with the R package mirt [@chalmers2012].

The retained scoring model was a GRM with rater-specific discriminations and thresholds [@samejima1969], also estimated in mirt. Its thresholds are ordered by construction. The GRM was estimated by marginal maximum likelihood with the EM algorithm and 61 quadrature points; standard errors were obtained with Oakes' identity [@chalmers2018]. The model converged after 165 iterations, and the information matrix was positive definite (@tbl-grm-convergence). [\[FILL IN: convergence tolerance, which is displayed as 0.000 in the table (FI-6)\]]{.mark}

## Model comparison

Within the nested ladder, two likelihood-ratio (LR) tests were computed: M1 versus M2 tested rater-specific thresholds, and M2 versus M3 tested rater-specific discriminations. For all four models, the log-likelihood, the Akaike (AIC) and Bayesian (BIC) information criteria and the sample-size adjusted BIC (SABIC) were computed, together with the difference to the best model on each criterion. Because the GRM and the ladder belong to different families and are not nested, the GRM was compared with the ladder by information criteria only.

Three features of this comparison need to be noted. First, the M1–M2 test compares models estimated in different software (sirt and mirt). The two packages may differ in quadrature and constants, so the test is approximate and the nesting is assumed rather than shown. Second, the degrees of freedom of the M1–M2 test are below the formula value. The formula $(J-1)(K-2)$, with $J$ raters and $K$ categories, assumes that every rater used all seven categories. A rater who never used an end category has one step parameter fewer in M2, so the observed degrees of freedom are smaller by the number of unused end categories, which are listed per rater in @tbl-category-usage. Third, no model without rater severity was fitted, so differences in severity were not tested formally.

## Model adequacy

Model adequacy was examined with three rater-level statistics and one global statistic. Infit and outfit mean squares [@wright1982] were computed for each rater under M1 and under the GRM. Their expected value is 1, and no misfit cut-offs were applied. With about two ratings per product, values below 1 are expected, because each product's score is estimated from the very ratings being checked. The S-X² item-fit statistic [@orlando2000; @kang2008] requires complete data; the missing ratings were therefore imputed 20 times from the fitted model, and the statistic was averaged over the imputations. About 90% of the cells were imputed. Because the imputed cells come from the fitted model itself, the test has little power to detect misfit. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-11\]]{.mark}

Local dependence was examined with Yen's Q3 [@yen1984], the correlation of two raters' residuals over the products both rated. Because Q3 is negatively biased when few raters rate each product [@christensen2017], rater pairs were compared by the deviation of their Q3 from the mean Q3 over all computable pairs. A pair was flagged when it had at least 30 jointly rated products and its Q3 deviated from the mean Q3 by more than 0.2. This flag criterion has no reference distribution.

Global fit was to be assessed with the limited-information statistic C2 [@cai2014]. C2 could not be computed: it needs the joint distribution of every rater pair, which is undefined for the 17 of 171 rater pairs that share no products.

## Scores and reliability

Product scores were expected a posteriori (EAP) estimates $\hat\theta$, with the posterior standard deviation (PSD) as their conditional standard error. The primary reliability index for the obtained scores was the empirical marginal reliability, $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta) / [\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta) + \overline{\mathrm{PSD}^2}]$, which refers to the scores actually obtained. For comparison, the model-based marginal reliability [@green1984] was computed with mirt; it refers to a hypothetical product rated by all raters. A computation on a grid of $\theta$ values served as a check.

Ninety-five percent intervals for both reliabilities were obtained from 200 accepted draws of the model parameters from their asymptotic normal distribution, defined by the estimates and the Oakes covariance matrix. For the empirical reliability, products were also resampled in each draw. A draw was rejected and replaced when it did not define a valid GRM, that is, when some discrimination was $\leq 0$ or some rater's thresholds were out of order; 87 draws were rejected and replaced. The intervals are therefore conditional on valid parameter sets and are approximate, especially for raters with few ratings. [\[FILL IN: optional analyst action - which raters caused the rejected draws; draws on a transformed scale; more accepted draws (FI-28)\]]{.mark}

To examine how reliability depends on the number of ratings per product and on which raters give them, reliability was projected from the fitted GRM. Products with $\theta \sim N(0, 1)$ were simulated; each received $k$ ratings ($k$ = 1 to 10) drawn from the fitted GRM and was scored with the fitted parameters. The raters were either drawn at random for each product, or fixed to the $k$ most or the $k$ least informative raters, ranked by their average information (see Rater parameters, information and response styles). The simulation used 50 replications of 2000 simulated products per $k$ and rater set (seed 20260713). Three measures were computed for each $k$ and rater set: the empirical marginal reliability (as for the real scores), the squared correlation with the true $\theta$, and the mean product-level reliability; bands are the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles over replications. Model parameters are treated as known in this projection. Its bands therefore reflect simulation variability only, not parameter uncertainty, and are not the same kind of interval as the parameter-draw intervals above.

At the product level, two reliability indices were computed. The posterior-based index was rel~post~ $= 1 - \mathrm{PSD}^2$. Because it is defined relative to the unit prior variance of $\theta$, rel~post~ partly reflects the prior when a product has only one or two ratings. The information-based index was rel~info~ $= I/(I+1)$, where $I$ is the information that the product's own raters provide at its $\hat\theta$. The agreement of the two indices served as a consistency check, and both were summarised descriptively by the number of ratings each product actually received; these observed summaries were not used for planning.

As reference values for common practice, which were not used in any further analysis, three conventional indices were computed. Cronbach's alpha [@cronbach1951] was computed from pairwise covariances over all usable raters and, alternatively, on the largest fully crossed block of raters and products. [\[FILL IN: why five raters (R19, R14, R02, R16, R12) were not usable for the pairwise alpha; optionally, which three raters form the crossed block (FI-9)\]]{.mark} Krippendorff's ordinal alpha [@hayes2007] measured the agreement of single ratings. Ninety-five percent confidence intervals were obtained by bootstrapping products (1000 replications). For the pairwise Cronbach's alpha, replications in which some rater pair lost all shared products could not be computed; 361 of the 1000 replications failed, and the interval is based on the remaining replications. Because the successful replications are not a random subset of all resamples, this interval is approximate and may also be biased. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-11\]]{.mark} On the choice of reliability indices in incomplete rating designs, see @tenhove2024.

## Rater parameters, information and response styles

For each rater, the GRM discrimination $a$ and thresholds $b_k$ were reported with their standard errors. Rater information was integrated over the standard normal distribution of $\theta$; we call this quantity the rater's average information. Each rater's share of the information of the full panel was computed both as a weighted share over $\theta$ and at selected values of $\theta$. Ninety-five percent intervals for average information and shares were obtained from the same parameter draws as the reliability intervals, with the same caveat: they are conditional on valid draws and approximate for raters with few ratings.

Descriptive response styles were computed on the raw 1–7 scale: each rater's mean, standard deviation, number of categories used, entropy (natural logarithm), floor rate (share of ratings of 1), ceiling rate (share of ratings of 7), extreme rate (ratings of 1 or 7) and central rate (ratings of 3–5). These descriptives are not adjusted for which products each rater saw.

## Score agreement and sensitivity

To examine RQ3(b), each product's raw mean rating, the common-practice score that treats raters as interchangeable, was compared with its GRM score, overall and by the number of ratings per product (1, 2, 3 or more). Because the raw mean has many ties (with one rating it takes only seven values) and tied products share one percentile rank, the comparison relied on tie-aware statistics: Pearson and Spearman correlations; Kendall's $\tau_b$; the share of discordant pairs, that is, among product pairs with different raw means, the share that the GRM score orders the other way round; the share of products changing quintile when raw-mean ties are ordered by the GRM score, which is the smallest change any tie-breaking can give; the share of products whose raw mean is shared by another product; and the mean and maximum range of GRM scores among products with the same raw mean. The table also lists the plain share of products changing quintile and the shifts in percentile rank, which overstate the disagreement because of ties; these are not used in the text. [\[FILL IN: whether percentiles and quintiles in the 1 / 2 / 3+ groups were computed within each group or over all products; how the groups of equal raw mean were formed in the pooled row, and how many and how large they are; the number of pairs behind the share of discordant pairs (FI-20)\]]{.mark}

To examine how strongly the product scores depend on the choice among the four models, the EAP scores of all models were correlated (Pearson and Spearman). Relative to the GRM, the absolute shift in percentile rank (on a 0–1 scale) and the shares of products changing quintile and changing by two or more quintiles were computed. The raw-mean comparison and the model comparison rest on different statistics and are reported separately. M1 was additionally re-estimated with the default integration grid of sirt as a check. Finally, the sensitivity of the GRM results to the rater exclusion was examined by refitting the GRM with all 22 raters.

## Software and availability

All models were estimated in R with the packages mirt [@chalmers2012] and sirt [@robitzsch2025]; psych and a Krippendorff package were used for the conventional indices, and Python was used for display. # Results

As outlined in the Introduction, the analyses addressed three aims: how the reliability of the scores depends on the number of ratings and on the raters who give them, how raters differ, and how much the scores depend on whether rater differences are modelled. All analyses used the final data in @tbl-design-summary. In this section, we first report the scoring model, then the reliability of the scores, the rater differences, the comparisons of scoring approaches, and the sensitivity to the rater exclusion.

## Scoring model

As can be seen in @tbl-model-fit, the GRM had the lowest AIC, BIC and SABIC of the four models. The GRM and M3 have the same number of parameters (127), so that their comparison reduces to the log-likelihood, which was −11733.227 for the GRM and −11756.510 for M3, a difference of 46.566 on all three criteria. The differences for M1 and M2 are given in the table. The GRM converged after 165 EM iterations with a positive definite information matrix (@tbl-grm-convergence).

The rater-level fit statistics of the GRM are given in @tbl-grm-rater-fit. No rater's S-X² was significant (*p* from .294 to .671). Infit ranged from 0.334 (R19) to 0.971 (R18) and outfit from 0.322 (R19) to 0.961 (R18); all values were below 1. The mean Q3 over 137 computable rater pairs was −.238, and 20 pairs were flagged; @tbl-grm-q3-flagged shows the 10 of them with the largest deviation from the mean Q3, of which nine deviated negatively and one (R10–R11) positively. C2 could not be computed. The informative value of these statistics is limited, as described under Model adequacy.

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#tbl-model-fit >}}

## Number of ratings, choice of raters and reliability of the creativity scores

@fig-grm-reliability-projection plots the projected empirical marginal reliability against the number of ratings per product for the three rater sets; the values are listed in @tbl-grm-reliability-projection. In all three sets, projected reliability rose with every additional rating. With randomly drawn raters, it was .508 for one rating, .688 for two, .857 for five and .925 for ten ratings. With the most informative raters, it rose from .754 for one rating to .947 for ten, and with the least informative raters from .108 to .884. At every number of ratings, the most informative raters gave the highest and the least informative raters the lowest values, and the gap between the sets narrowed as the number of ratings increased (one rating: .754, .508 and .108; five: .920, .857 and .701; ten: .947, .925 and .884). One rating from the most informative raters (.754) gave a higher projected reliability than two ratings from randomly drawn raters (.688). The other two measures, the squared correlation with the true $\theta$ and the mean product-level reliability, agreed with the empirical value to within .003 in every row. No projected value reached the model-based full-panel reliability of .960; the highest was .947.

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#fig-grm-reliability-projection >}}

Three qualifications apply to the projection. The model parameters are treated as known, so that the bands reflect only the variability over 50 simulation replications; the raters that form the most and least informative sets are not listed in the output; and the projection covers one to ten ratings per product only.

@tbl-reliability-overview contrasts the reliability of the scores actually obtained with the other indices and states what each refers to. The empirical marginal reliability of the obtained scores was .672 [.649, .687]. The model-based marginal reliability, which refers to a hypothetical product rated by all raters, was .960 [.953, .968], with a grid check of .960 (@tbl-grm-reliability-ci; @fig-grm-panel-information). Of the conventional indices, Cronbach's alpha from pairwise covariances was .928 [.891, .943] (14 raters, 1900 products); this interval is approximate (see Scores and reliability; @tbl-naive-indices). On the fully crossed block, Cronbach's alpha was .658 [.526, .756] (3 raters, 139 products). Krippendorff's ordinal alpha, which refers to the agreement of single ratings, was .392 [.362, .417] (19 raters, 2771 products).

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#tbl-reliability-overview >}}

The observed product-level reliability is summarised descriptively by the number of ratings each product received in @tbl-grm-reliability-by-n and @fig-grm-rel-post-by-n. Mean rel~post~ was .520 for the 897 products with one rating, .698 for the 2080 products with two and .810 for the 125 products with four ratings; the full series, up to .919 for the three products with ten ratings, is given in the table. The mean PSD fell from 0.686 to 0.285 across these groups. Products with the same number of ratings differed in rel~post~ (@fig-grm-rel-post-by-n), and the relation of rel~post~ to the products' $\hat\theta$ is shown in @fig-grm-rel-post-by-theta. These values are observational: products were not assigned a number of ratings at random, and the means have no confidence intervals.

Across all products, rel~post~ had a median of .698 and an interquartile range of .173 (Q1 .596, Q3 .769), with values from .057 to .929 (@tbl-grm-reliability-summary; @fig-grm-rel-post-histogram). The two product-level indices correlated at *r* = .935, and 320 products differed by more than .1 (@fig-grm-rel-consistency).

## Rater differences

@fig-overview-rater-response-styles gives a descriptive first view of the raters on the raw scale, not adjusted for which products each rater saw. Rater means ranged from 1.760 (R06) to 3.836 (R18), and standard deviations from 1.022 (R01) to 1.953 (R19). The floor rate ranged from .579 (R06) to .016 (R13). The ceiling rate was highest for R19 (.080), and five raters (R06, R17, R01, R03 and R18) had a ceiling rate of .000. The central rate (ratings of 3–5) was high for R13 (.799) and R12 (.735) and low for R06 (.192). Across all ratings, the ratings concentrated at the low end of the scale: category 1 received 2029 ratings and category 2 received 2113, whereas category 7 was the rarest, with 109 ratings (@fig-overview-rating-distribution). As noted in the Methods, five raters left top categories unused.

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/01_data_overview.ipynb#fig-overview-rater-response-styles >}}

The GRM parameters in @tbl-grm-rater-parameters show the raters on the latent scale, together with their standard errors. Among the raters with at least 400 ratings (R01–R09), a grouping we use for description only, first thresholds $b_1$ ranged from −2.21 (R09, *SE* 0.36) to 0.29 (R06, *SE* 0.06); R13 (254 ratings) had a first threshold of −3.38 (*SE* 0.49). R06 was the only rater with a positive first threshold. Threshold spacing also differed, for example from −0.71 ($b_1$) to 2.03 ($b_6$) for R02 and from −3.38 to 4.43 for R13; as described under Measurement models, spacing in the GRM is partly the same fact as discrimination. R18's thresholds had the largest standard errors (*SE* of $b_1$ 3.05). R17 had four thresholds, R01, R03, R06 and R18 had five, and all other raters had six. The category response functions are shown in @fig-grm-category-response-functions.

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#tbl-grm-rater-parameters >}}

Among the raters with at least 400 ratings, discrimination ranged from 0.86 (R09, *SE* 0.15) to 2.81 (R06, *SE* 0.42); R01 had 1.96 (*SE* 0.16) and R02 2.50 (*SE* 0.33), and R13 (254 ratings) had 1.50 (*SE* 0.22). The two highest estimates, 3.71 for R19 (*SE* 2.22) and 3.70 for R16 (*SE* 1.36), came from raters with 50 and 52 ratings and had the largest standard errors; the lowest estimate, 0.63 for R18 (*SE* 0.26), also came from a rater with few ratings (55).

The average information of each rater and their share of the full-panel information are given with 95% intervals in @tbl-grm-rater-information-ci. For raters with many ratings, average information was, for example, 0.238 [0.110, 0.419] for R09, 0.979 [0.723, 1.219] for R01 and 1.705 [0.903, 2.558] for R02, with shares of .037 [.022, .050] for R01 and .065 [.035, .098] for R02. The widest intervals belonged to raters with about 50 ratings, for example R19, with an average information of 3.539 [0.410, 11.017] and a share of .135 [.017, .331], and R16, with 3.300 [0.728, 6.489].

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#tbl-grm-rater-information-ci >}}

Raters provided information in different regions of the latent scale (@fig-grm-rater-information; @tbl-grm-information-summary). The location of maximum information was highest for R01 (2.700) and R06 (2.400) and lowest for R13 (−0.550). The shares of the panel information varied with $\theta$ (@fig-grm-information-shares): R06 contributed .001 at $\theta = -2$ but .083 at $\theta = +2$, whereas R12 contributed .221 at $\theta = -2$. The intervals for information and shares rest on the same 200 accepted parameter draws as the reliability intervals; the raw response-style indices have no per-rater uncertainty.

## How much do the scores depend on modelling rater differences?

The constraints that treat raters as equivalent were examined first. The LR test of M1 against M2, which concerns a shared category structure, gave $\chi^2(84) = 737.457$, *p* < .001 (@tbl-lr-tests). The test of M2 against M3, which concerns equal discrimination, gave $\chi^2(18) = 121.958$, *p* < .001. AIC also favoured M3 over M2 (23767.020 vs. 23852.978), whereas BIC ranked M2 (24529.585) below M3 (24555.360) (@tbl-model-fit). Rater-specific discriminations were thus supported by the LR test and AIC, but not by BIC.

Three further results describe the constrained models. Under M3, discriminations ranged from 0.283 (R09, *SE* 0.055) to 2.606 (R16, *SE* 1.419) (@tbl-discrimination-m3). Nine raters had unordered step parameters under M2, and nine under M3 (@tbl-threshold-order); the GRM thresholds are ordered by construction. Under M1, only R17 (infit 1.328, outfit 1.190) and R18 (infit 1.009, outfit 1.071) had values at or above 1, and R12 had the lowest values (infit 0.238, outfit 0.255; @tbl-rater-fit-m1).

@tbl-raw-mean-vs-grm and @fig-raw-mean-vs-theta compare the raw mean rating of each product with its GRM score. Over all 3668 products, Kendall's $\tau_b$ was .796, and a share of .083 of the product pairs with different raw means were ordered the other way round by the GRM score. With raw-mean ties ordered by the GRM score, a share of .237 of products still changed quintile, the smallest change any tie-breaking can give. The Pearson and Spearman correlations were .906 and .932. Nearly every product shared its raw mean with another product (.995).

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#tbl-raw-mean-vs-grm >}}

Products rated once are the simplest case. Products with the same single rating received GRM scores up to 1.436 apart (mean range 1.283); among these products, .042 of the pairs were discordant, and .104 changed quintile with ties resolved. In the 1-rating panel of @fig-raw-mean-vs-theta, the GRM scores at a given single rating spread vertically; the points are jittered horizontally. Across the groups, the pattern was mixed: the correlations and $\tau_b$ were highest for products with three or more ratings (Pearson .954, Spearman .959, $\tau_b$ = .842), whereas the shares of discordant pairs and of tie-resolved quintile changes were lowest for products with one rating; the shares were .067 and .220 for two ratings and .070 and .220 for three or more ratings. The maximum range of GRM scores among products with the same raw mean was 1.436, 2.196 and 1.396 in the groups with one, two, and three or more ratings. The groups were not compared by a statistical test.

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#fig-raw-mean-vs-theta >}}

@tbl-score-agreement shows how the product scores of the constrained models differ from the GRM scores. Relative to the GRM, the scores of M1 correlated at .975 (Pearson) and .978 (Spearman), with a mean absolute percentile shift of .042; a share of .202 of products changed quintile and .004 changed by two or more quintiles. For M2, the corresponding values were .985, .983, .033, .150 and .003, and for M3 .996, .996, .017, .075 and .001. Among the ladder models, Pearson correlations ranged from .980 to .993 and Spearman correlations from .983 to .996 (@tbl-theta-correlations). M1 re-estimated with the default integration grid correlated at 1.000 with M1.

{{< embed ../data-analysis/creativity-ratings-psychometrics/notebooks/02_jrt_results.ipynb#tbl-score-agreement >}}

Several qualifications apply to these comparisons. No confidence intervals are available for the correlations, the agreement statistics or the raw-mean comparison. The contrast between M1 and the GRM combines the rater constraints with a change of link function, whereas M3 and the GRM have the same number of parameters and differ only in the link. Finally, all shifts are differences from the GRM; they show that the scores differ, not which score is more accurate.

## Sensitivity to the rater exclusion

Refitting the GRM with all 22 raters (7844 ratings, 3669 products) changed the empirical marginal reliability from .67199 to .67186 and the model-based marginal reliability from .95986 to .96186 (@tbl-sensitivity-rater-exclusion). Over the 3668 common products, the scores of the two fits correlated at .99997 (Pearson) and .99996 (Spearman); the mean absolute difference was 0.00171, the maximum 0.16246, and a share of .00491 of products changed quintile. Over the 19 common raters, the discriminations correlated at .99880, with a maximum absolute difference of 0.19820. No confidence intervals are available for these differences.

# Discussion

This study set out to describe how the reliability of creativity scores for football actions depends on the number of ratings and on the raters who give them, how raters differ, and how much the scores depend on whether rater differences are modelled. The reliability of the obtained scores was below that of a hypothetical full panel, and in the projection from the fitted model, reliability rose with the number of ratings per product and depended on which raters gave them. Raters differed in threshold location, category use, discrimination and information, with imprecise estimates for raters with few ratings. The constraints that treat raters as equivalent in category structure and discrimination were rejected by the LR tests, and for discrimination also by AIC but not by BIC. Raw mean scores and GRM scores ordered a non-trivial share of products differently, and the choice among the models also shifted rankings. These results rest on the GRM, which described the ratings best by all information criteria.

## How many ratings per action, and from whom?

The conventional figures describe the mean of a large or complete panel: the model-based full-panel reliability was .960 and the pairwise Cronbach's alpha .928. The scores that were actually obtained, however, had an empirical reliability of .672 [.649, .687], and this is the figure that matters for any downstream use of the scores. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-3\]]{.mark} This difference follows the Spearman–Brown logic described by @amabile1982: reliability depends on the number of ratings that are aggregated, and the panel coefficients refer to more ratings per product than the products actually received. The contrast between Krippendorff's alpha for single ratings (.392) and the pairwise Cronbach's alpha (.928) illustrates the point made by @kaufman2008 that a high alpha can hide low agreement between individual raters. The alpha on the fully crossed block (.658, three raters) lay close to the empirical reliability, although the two indices refer to different quantities and this closeness should not be read as equivalence. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-13\]]{.mark}

The projection provides the planning evidence for the number of ratings. Under the fitted model, reliability rose with each additional rating, and it depended strongly on which raters gave the ratings. One rating from the most informative raters gave a higher projected reliability (.754) than two ratings from randomly drawn raters (.688), and ten ratings from the least informative raters (.884) stayed below three ratings from the most informative raters (.892). In these data, who rates therefore matters as much as how many. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-24: framing that links RQ1 and RQ2\]]{.mark} This links the first aim to the second: the rater differences described under RQ2 are what make the choice of raters matter for reliability. With @cseh2019, who argue that the number of raters must be established for each domain, the projection gives such values for this football rating task and this rater pool. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-4, ATC-5; see ATC-2 on novelty\]]{.mark} Because the projection treats the model parameters as known, its bands understate the uncertainty of these values.

The observed reliability by number of ratings (@tbl-grm-reliability-by-n) describes the products as they were rated. In the analysis notebook, this observed relation is described as confounded, because products with more ratings were also rated by different raters. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-25\]]{.mark} We therefore use the projection, not the observed values, for planning. Taken together, the precision of a product's score depends on its number of ratings, on which raters gave them and on where the product lies on $\theta$ relative to its raters' thresholds (@fig-grm-rel-post-by-theta; @fig-grm-rater-information). [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-4\]]{.mark} Because rel~post~ is defined relative to a unit prior variance, its values for products with one or two ratings partly reflect the prior. For reporting, these results imply that creativity studies should report the reliability of the scores actually used, that is, the empirical marginal reliability and product standard errors, and not only alpha or full-panel values. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-15\]]{.mark}

## Raters differ

The raters spanned a wide range of threshold locations, category use and discrimination. For raters with many ratings, the differences in discrimination clearly exceeded the standard errors, for example between R09 (0.86, *SE* 0.15) and R06 (2.81, *SE* 0.42). [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-6\]]{.mark} Because threshold spacing in the GRM is partly the same fact as discrimination, wide or narrow spacing is not separate evidence of scale use; the raw response styles provide scale-use evidence that does not depend on the model, with the caveat that they are not adjusted for which products each rater saw. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-6\]]{.mark} These differences are in line with reports of differing scale use and beliefs about creativity among CAT raters [@long2015] and with the rater effects described in rater-mediated assessment, such as severity, central tendency and restriction of range [@engelhard1994; @myford2003; @myford2004]. The contrast between raters who concentrated their ratings in the middle categories (e.g., R13) and raters who used the floor category heavily (e.g., R06) corresponds to the preference for central or extreme categories discussed by @myszkowski2021. @primi2019 left such interactions between raters and the rating scale to future research; the present results describe them for ratings of football actions. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-6\]]{.mark}

The uncertainty of these estimates needs to be considered. Wide intervals mean that a rater's informativeness is not yet well determined, which was typically the case for raters with few ratings. For the raters with about 50 ratings, R16 and R19, the highest discriminations and information shares came with the widest intervals, so that the information shares are not a ranking of rater quality. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-12\]]{.mark} The parameter-draw intervals are, moreover, conditional on valid draws and approximate for these raters. This is consistent with work showing that rater estimates in incomplete rating networks depend on the linking set [@wind2018; @wind2019a] and that GRM parameter recovery requires adequate numbers of responses [@reise1990]. Which rater characteristics predict discernment is a separate question [@ceh2022]. Finally, raters informed different regions of the latent scale: R06 was most informative at high creativity, whereas R12 contributed the largest share at low creativity. This is relevant for assigning raters to products. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-16\]]{.mark}

## Why rater differences matter for scoring creativity in sport

Three kinds of rater difference bear on scoring, and they need to be kept apart. The first is severity. Unweighted means treat raters as interchangeable, and when different raters rate different actions, the means are confounded with rater severity [@primi2019]. In these data, the clearest case is a single rating: the same rating corresponded to GRM scores up to 1.436 apart (@fig-raw-mean-vs-theta). With one rating, a product's GRM score depends only on that rating and on the parameters of the rater who gave it, so that this spread reflects differences between raters as modelled. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-21\]]{.mark} In the words of the analysis notebook, products with the same raw mean get different GRM scores when they were rated by raters of different severity or discrimination. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-21: this is the explanation given in the analysis notebook, not a tested result\]]{.mark} Severity differences as such were not tested formally, because no model without a severity facet was fitted. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-7\]]{.mark}

The second and third kinds are category structure and discrimination, which the MFRM still constrains after severity has been modelled. Both constraints were rejected by the LR tests, and rater-specific discriminations were supported by the LR test and AIC, but not by BIC. These tests concern the Rasch and MFRM constraints, not raw-mean averaging directly. Part of the observed heterogeneity in discrimination may be estimation noise for raters with few ratings, whose standard errors were largest under both M3 and the GRM. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-7\]]{.mark} The fit of the raters under M1 is consistent with the account that the MFRM expresses differences in discrimination only as misfit [@myford2004; @myszkowski2021]: R17, with values above 1 under M1, had a comparatively low GRM discrimination (1.45), whereas R12, with the lowest values under M1, had a high GRM discrimination (2.90). Because no cut-offs were applied, this pattern describes values above and below 1 rather than misfitting raters. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-9\]]{.mark} The GRM was preferred by all information criteria. A cumulative link is plausible for a unipolar creativity scale, and @pellegrino2025 also retained a GRM for creativity ratings. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-8\]]{.mark} Neither the unordered steps in M2 and M3 nor the ordered GRM thresholds count as evidence for either family, because unordered steps in adjacent-category models indicate only that some category is never the most likely response [@andrich1978; @bond2020], and GRM thresholds are ordered by construction. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-9\]]{.mark}

These differences have consequences for the scores. Raw mean ratings and GRM scores agreed only partly: Kendall's $\tau_b$ was .796, .083 of the product pairs with different raw means were ordered the other way round, and at least .237 of products fell into a different quintile. In applications that select actions, for example the top quintile of creative actions for training material, such differences are consequential. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-22\]]{.mark} The choice of scoring model also mattered: although all correlations between the models were .975 or higher, .202 of products changed quintile between the MFRM/RSM and the GRM, and .075 between the GPCM and the GRM. Because the MFRM–GRM contrast combines the rater constraints with a change of link function, the two sources cannot be separated in this comparison. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-10\]]{.mark} The two comparisons rest on different statistics and are not ranked against each other here. These results agree with the observation of @primi2019 that means are confounded with rater severity in incomplete designs, and with the argument of @myszkowski2019 against the assumption of $\tau$-equivalence. What the comparisons do not show is that the GRM scores are more accurate. The GRM is not a validated criterion: it adjusts for the modelled rater differences, but whether it predicts unseen ratings better than the raw mean was not tested. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-15, ATC-22\]]{.mark}

## Practical implications for creativity research in sport

The following implications are drawn from one pool of student raters and one 7-point scale, and they may not transfer unchanged to other rater pools. [\[FILL IN: rater-pool description to qualify this scope (FI-21)\]]{.mark} First, the number of ratings per action, and the raters who give them, can be planned for a target score reliability. A projection from a fitted rater model, such as @fig-grm-reliability-projection, shows how reliability grows with each additional rating and how much it depends on the raters chosen. The present projection treats the parameters as known, refers to this rater pool and this scale, covers up to ten ratings per action (i.e., per product), and will be refreshed when more ratings have been collected. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-5, ATC-24\]]{.mark}

Second, a calibration set of actions rated by all raters would link the raters, make their parameters comparable and stabilise the discriminations of raters with few ratings [@wind2019a; @forthmann2023]; it would also make fully crossed reliability and absolute fit checks estimable. Such a calibration set is distinct from rater training, which conflicts with the CAT rule of independent judgement without imposed criteria [@hennessey2011; @dollinger2005; @storme2014]. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-14\]]{.mark}

Third, rater differences should be modelled rather than averaged. JRT scores with their posterior standard deviations can replace raw means; the raw-mean comparison shows that this choice changes the ordering of actions, although it does not show that the JRT score is more accurate. The empirical marginal reliability and the product standard errors should be reported and carried into downstream analyses. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-15, ATC-22\]]{.mark}

Fourth, rater workload and assignment deserve planning. In these data, raters with about 50 ratings still had imprecise parameters, so each rater should give enough ratings for stable rater parameters. Rater information functions could additionally inform the assignment of raters to actions. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-16\]]{.mark}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Design recommendations for creativity ratings in sport"}
1. Plan the number of ratings per action, and who gives them, from the reliability you need; a projection from a fitted rater model shows both (see @fig-grm-reliability-projection). [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-23, ATC-5, ATC-24\]]{.mark}
2. Let all raters rate a common calibration set of actions, so that raters are linked and their parameters are comparable. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-23, ATC-14\]]{.mark}
3. Give each rater enough ratings for stable rater parameters; in these data, about 50 ratings per rater still left the parameters imprecise (see @tbl-grm-rater-parameters and @tbl-grm-rater-information-ci). [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-23, ATC-16\]]{.mark}
4. Score actions with a model that adjusts for rater differences rather than with the raw mean rating, and report how much the ordering changes (see @tbl-raw-mean-vs-grm). [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-23, ATC-15, ATC-22\]]{.mark}
5. Report the reliability of the scores actually used (empirical marginal reliability, product standard errors), not only alpha or full-panel values (see @tbl-reliability-overview). [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-23, ATC-3, ATC-15\]]{.mark}
:::

## Limitations and future research

Several limitations qualify these results. First, the rating design was incomplete: not every rater rated every product, and the analysis assumes that the missing ratings are ignorable given the allocation of products to raters. [\[FILL IN: allocation procedure (FI-4)\]]{.mark} Ratings marked "action not recognised" were removed; if non-recognition depended on the action or on the rater, the missingness would not be ignorable. [\[FILL IN: non-recognition rate by rater (FI-22)\]]{.mark} The observed reliability by number of ratings is observational; the projection addresses this, but it rests on the fitted model (see the second and third limitations).

Second, the fit evidence is limited by the design. S-X² has little power because most cells are imputed from the fitted model; C2 could not be computed because some rater pairs share no products; Q3 is negatively biased when few raters rate each product [@christensen2017], and the flag criterion has no reference distribution; and infit and outfit values below 1 are expected when each product's score is estimated from the same few ratings. The absence of detected misfit is therefore not evidence of fit, and the GRM is the best-fitting of the compared models rather than a validated reference. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-11\]]{.mark} A calibration set rated by all raters would make these checks considerably more informative, and a held-out-rating check could compare the predictive accuracy of the scores.

Third, the parameters of raters with few ratings are imprecise, and the parameter-draw intervals are conditional on valid draws and approximate for these raters. The projection treats the parameters as known, so that its bands understate the uncertainty. A standard normal latent distribution was assumed; the EAP scores, rel~post~ and the projection depend on it, and the ratings were concentrated at the low end of the scale. A check with a more flexible latent distribution was not carried out. The response-style indices are raw descriptives without uncertainty.

Fourth, the raters formed a single pool of students, and no rater covariates were analysed. [\[FILL IN: rater-pool characteristics (FI-1, FI-21)\]]{.mark} Whether these raters meet the CAT's requirement of familiarity with the domain is not established here, so the projection, the rater differences and the recommendations may be specific to this pool. The role of expertise is not analysed in this paper and remains a question for future work [@kaufman2009; @kaufman2013; @ceh2022]. Fifth, raters with fewer than 15 ratings were excluded as a technical estimation criterion; the largest change in a product score from this exclusion was 0.16246 (@tbl-sensitivity-rater-exclusion). [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-26\]]{.mark}

Sixth, the model comparison has caveats: the M1–M2 test compares models estimated in different software, so that the likelihoods may not be on exactly the same scale and the nesting is assumed rather than shown, and its degrees of freedom are below the formula value because of unused end categories; severity differences were not tested formally; BIC disagreed with the LR test and AIC on discrimination; the score-agreement contrasts mix rater constraints and link function; and the raw-mean comparison has no confidence intervals, and its grouping definitions remain to be documented. Seventh, the models included two facets and one dimension only. They contain no facet for time, session or fatigue, although rater tendencies can drift [@barth2020; @leckie2011; @myford2009] and workload affects agreement [@forthmann2017], and they do not test differential rater functioning [@wind2019b]. Rater models with additional structure, such as the hierarchical rater model [@patz2002] or generalized many-facet models [@uto2020], could address these extensions. Unidimensionality was assumed, and only the creativity dimension was analysed.

Future work should therefore use a prospective design with a calibration set rated by all raters, extend the projection to include parameter uncertainty and other rater pools [@forthmann2023], validate model-based against raw-mean scores, for example on held-out ratings, include rater covariates such as football expertise, and replicate the analysis in other sports.

# Conclusion

In these data, the reliability of the creativity scores actually obtained for football actions was far below the figures conventionally reported for a full panel, and the projection from the fitted model showed that it depends on both the number of ratings per action and the raters who give them. Raters differed in threshold location, category use, discrimination and information. Constraints that treat raters as equivalent in category structure and discrimination were rejected, and both raw mean scoring and constrained models ordered actions differently from the GRM. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-1\]]{.mark} For rater pools of this kind, creativity research in sport should plan the number of ratings per action and the choice of raters with a model-based projection, link raters through a common calibration set, and model rater differences with judge response theory instead of averaging ratings. [\[AUTHOR TO CONFIRM; ATC-5, ATC-14, ATC-15, ATC-24\]]{.mark}
